approved: Fair Work Amendment (Repeal of 4 Yearly Reviews and Other Measures) Bill 2017
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record

This bill would change the Fair Work Act to act on two recommendations from the Productivity Commission's workplace relations report and two from a separate inquiry into a Fair Work Commission member.

It would remove the requirement for the Fair Work Commission to conduct four-yearly reviews of modern awards, and allow the commission to ignore minor procedural or technical mistakes when approving enterprise agreements if those mistakes did not disadvantage employees.

The bill would also extend the complaint-handling powers of the Employment Minister and the Fair Work Commission President to former members of the Australian Industrial Relations Commission, and apply the Judicial Misbehaviour and Incapacity (Parliamentary Commissions) Act 2012 to current Fair Work Commission members.
Repeal the requirement for four-yearly reviews of modern awards from 1 January 2018.
Enable the Fair Work Commission to overlook minor procedural or technical errors in enterprise agreement approvals.
Extend complaint-handling powers to former AIRC members now serving on the Fair Work Commission.
Apply the Judicial Misbehaviour and Incapacity (Parliamentary Commissions) Act 2012 to Fair Work Commission members.
The Fair Work Commission, its members, employers, employees, and the Minister for Employment would be affected.

The government introduced the Fair Work Amendment (Repeal of 4 Yearly Reviews and Other Measures) Bill 2017, proposing to repeal mandatory four-yearly reviews of modern awards (saving $87 million over 10 years), allow the Fair Work Commission to overlook minor procedural errors in enterprise bargaining, and strengthen accountability for Commission members following the Heerey inquiry into former Vice-President Michael Lawler.

The speaker moved a motion to suspend standing orders to allow the Fair Work Amendment (Repeal of 4 Yearly Reviews and Other Measures) Bill 2017 to be debated and passed immediately, with deadlines for amendments and finalisation set for 12 pm on 1 March 2017.

The member moved to suspend standing orders to force immediate debate and passage of the Fair Work Amendment (Repeal of 4 Yearly Reviews and Other Measures) Bill 2017, criticising the minister for calling the government's own legislative procedure a "union Labor stunt."

The speaker argued the government was slow to respond to the 2015 Productivity Commission report and only acted due to pressure from unions and employer groups. They moved a second reading amendment calling on the government to abandon support for cutting penalty rates, which would reduce pay for nearly 700,000 Australians by up to $77 a week, and to legislate to prevent that decision.

The speaker criticised the government for delaying the Fair Work Amendment (Repeal of 4 Yearly Reviews and Other Measures) Bill 2017, noting that unions and employer groups supported scrapping mandatory four-year reviews, and argued that the government has not acted to prevent the upcoming cut to penalty rates affecting 700,000 workers, with some losing up to $6,000 annually.

The speaker supported the Fair Work Amendment (Repeal of 4 Yearly Reviews and Other Measures) Bill 2017 with amendments, and argued that the government's failure to stop penalty rate cuts from 2 July will reduce pay for up to 700,000 workers by up to $77 a week, while also criticising delays in implementing Productivity Commission recommendations.

The speaker argued that the Fair Work Amendment (Repeal of 4 Yearly Reviews and Other Measures) Bill 2017 fails to address major issues such as penalty rate cuts affecting young people and women, underpayment of workers at Coles, Woolworths, Hungry Jack's, McDonald's and KFC, insecure work and casualisation, stagnant wages, and employers terminating enterprise agreements to force workers onto lower award conditions.

The government argued the bill would repeal the requirement for four-yearly reviews of modern awards, saving $87 million, allow the Fair Work Commission to overlook minor procedural errors in enterprise agreements if employees were not disadvantaged, and establish a formal mechanism for parliament to handle allegations of misbehaviour against Fair Work Commission members.

The speaker argued that the opposition's amendments on penalty rates are not relevant to the Fair Work Amendment (Repeal of 4 Yearly Reviews and Other Measures) Bill 2017 and should be ruled out of order, calling the move an attempt to insert a separate private members' bill into unrelated legislation.

The speaker argued that opposition amendments to the Fair Work Amendment Bill were a repeat of private members’ bills and a tactic to bypass the requirement for an absolute majority of 76 votes under standing orders.

The speaker opposed amendments to the Fair Work Amendment Bill, arguing that reducing Sunday penalty rates from double time to time-and-a-half supports jobs and small businesses like coffee shops. The speaker stated the government would oppose the amendments because they were only just seen and the government supports the bill.

The speaker rejected amendments to the Fair Work Amendment Bill, arguing that award wage and penalty rate decisions should remain with the independent Fair Work Commission rather than politicians, citing his experience as former CEO of the National Retail Association and the Commission's evidence-based reduction of penalty rates in four key awards to boost employment.

The member moved to disagree with the amendments, arguing they are inconsistent with the bill's objective to repeal four-yearly reviews and other measures. The House of Representatives does not accept the amendments.

The opposition will not insist on its amendments to restore penalty rates, allowing the Fair Work Amendment (Repeal of 4 Yearly Reviews and Other Measures) Bill 2017 to pass, but will pursue other avenues to restore penalty rates. The bill is supported by both the government and opposition, as well as employers and unions.
